rules.statement: In production code, keep a constructor-initialized collection as `new T(args) { … }` and never use the C# 14 preview `[with(args), …]` collection-expression-arguments form a non-pinned CSharpier may emit.
rules.why: The preview form fails the build under LangVersion=latest (CS8652); the pinned CSharpier check accepts the constructor form.
rules.check: Look for `[with(` collection expressions introduced in a diff.

rules.statement: In production code, use file-scoped namespaces, 4-space indentation, a trailing comma on every multi-line object/collection/enum member list, and LF line endings.
rules.why: This is the house style CSharpier enforces; the check fails files with CRLF endings.
rules.check: Block-scoped namespaces, missing trailing commas in multi-line lists, CRLF files.

rules.statement: In production code, start every hand-written C# file with the two-line header `// Copyright © NCode Group` and `// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0` followed by a blank line, with no `#region` and no year.
rules.why: .editorconfig sets it as file_header_template and IDE0073 fails the build on a missing or different header; generated code is exempt.
rules.check: New files lacking the exact header or adding a year/#region.

rules.statement: In production code, don't use banned APIs: no Newtonsoft.Json (use System.Text.Json), no sync-over-async, no `JsonDocument.Parse`, no legacy `JwtSecurityTokenHandler`/`JwtSecurityToken` (use `JsonWebTokenHandler`), no throwing `DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeSeconds`/`FromUnixTimeMilliseconds`, no lenient text encodings and no bare buffer sources.
rules.why: BannedApiAnalyzers (RS0030) bans them from the BannedSymbols files and fails the build.
rules.check: Usages of the listed APIs.

rules.statement: In production code, leave no unused `using` directives.
rules.why: IDE0005 is raised solution-wide and fails the build.
rules.check: Unused usings in changed files.

rules.statement: In production code, strip the UTF-8 BOM from every file `dotnet ef migrations add` generates.
rules.why: EF writes files with a BOM, but the repository's files are BOM-less (`charset = utf-8`).
rules.check: New or re-scaffolded migration, designer and snapshot files that begin with a BOM.

rules.statement: In production code before the first stable release, handle an EF Core model change by deleting and re-scaffolding the context's single `InitialCreate` migration, designer and snapshot, never by adding a second migration or one with raw SQL or seed-data changes.
rules.why: Each host context keeps one InitialCreate migration until the first stable release; tests fail any other migration, and the drift check fails un-migrated model changes.
rules.check: A diff that changes entities or configurations without re-scaffolding InitialCreate, or that adds an extra migration.

rules.statement: In production code, quote identifiers in raw SQL fragments in the EF model, e.g. `HasFilter("\"NormalizedDomainName\" IS NOT NULL")`.
rules.why: The schema uses PascalCase, and only applying the migration to Postgres catches an unquoted fragment; the drift gate cannot.
rules.check: HasFilter, HasComputedColumnSql, HasDefaultValueSql and similar strings with unquoted column names.

rules.statement: In production code, keep hand-written code in a database project outside the `Migrations/` folder.
rules.why: .editorconfig treats `Migrations/` as generated code, so analyzers and style rules don't cover it.
rules.check: New non-generated types or helpers added under Migrations/.

rules.statement: In production code, once a migration baseline exists, make every schema migration expand-only so the previous release keeps working, and mark raw SQL or seed-data migrations with `[ExpandMigration("why")]` or `[ContractMigration("why")]`, shipping a contract step one release after its expansion.
rules.why: Migrations run before the rollout, so the previous release must still work against the new schema; a test gate fails contracting or unclassified migrations.
rules.check: New migrations that drop or tighten existing schema, or raw SQL/data migrations without a classification attribute.

rules.statement: In production code, don't flag a parameter list as too long when it mirrors a well-known BCL shape (e.g. `ClaimsIdentity(authenticationType, nameType, roleType)`) or belongs to a private helper with a single call site.
rules.why: The family accepts those clumps; a parameter object isn't worth it there.
rules.check: Before raising a few-parameters finding, see whether the signature mirrors a BCL constructor or is a private single-call-site helper.

rules.statement: In production code, push store filtering into the database through an intent-named store method (e.g. `FindEnabledByScopesAsync`) instead of paging or loading everything and filtering in memory; keep generic paging for genuinely unfiltered reads.
rules.why: Filtering belongs in the DBMS, and filtered reads are named for their intent.
rules.check: Callers that page through a store or load all rows and then apply Where or other filters in memory.

rules.statement: In production code, give a sentinel key stored in `HttpContext.Items` or `AuthenticationProperties.Items` a package prefix and define it once instead of repeating the string literal.
rules.why: No repeated magic strings; a prefix avoids collisions with other components' items.
rules.check: Bare or repeated string keys used with Items dictionaries.

rules.statement: In production code, dispose every `HttpResponseMessage`, `Stream` and `IHttpClientFactory`-created `HttpClient` the code owns.
rules.why: Dispose what you own; leaving them undisposed leaks connections and resources.
rules.check: Results of SendAsync/GetAsync, opened streams and factory-created clients without using/Dispose.

rules.statement: In production code, parse JSON into a detached `JsonElement` named for what it holds (or `jsonElement`), never `document`.
rules.why: The family parses into detached elements rather than holding JsonDocuments, and the name should say what the element holds.
rules.check: Variables named `document` holding a JsonElement, or a JsonDocument kept around instead of a detached element.

rules.statement: In production code, read `JsonElement` members through the family's shared non-throwing extension helpers (`TryGetPropertyValue<T>`, `TryGetValue<T>`, `IsNullOrUndefined()`, `EmptyObject`/`OrEmptyObject()`) instead of hand-rolled `TryGetProperty` + `ValueKind` + `GetString()`/`GetInt64()` chains, bare `ValueKind == Null` checks, or re-parsing "{}".
rules.why: The helpers convert by ValueKind and never throw, whereas the bare getters throw on a mismatched kind.
rules.check: TryGetProperty followed by ValueKind comparisons and Get* calls, `JsonValueKind.Null` absence checks, or parsing "{}".

rules.statement: In production code, reject JSON parsed from wire input (a token header or payload, a request body) unless its `ValueKind` is `Object` before reading its properties.
rules.why: `JsonElement.TryGetProperty` throws InvalidOperationException on anything but an object, so untrusted input could fault the caller.
rules.check: Property reads on parsed wire JSON with no preceding `ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Object` check.

rules.statement: In production code, parse a date/time string only through the family's shared date-coercion helper (invariant culture, zone-less means UTC, out-of-range fails), never a hand-rolled `DateTime(Offset).TryParse`, and only where the value is declared to be a date, never to sniff whether an arbitrary string looks like one.
rules.why: One policy gives every package the same formats and values; lenient sniffing turns strings like "1.2" or "10:30" into dates and rewrites them.
rules.check: DateTime.TryParse/DateTimeOffset.TryParse calls, or date parsing applied to untyped string claims.

rules.statement: In production code, read an RFC 7519 NumericDate (`exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `auth_time`, Unix-seconds parameters) strictly with non-throwing, range-guarded readers (JSON numbers only, never strings), and fail closed when a time claim is present but invalid instead of treating it as absent.
rules.why: Wire input must never fault the caller, and an invalid time claim read as absent would bypass validation.
rules.check: Time-claim reads that accept strings, can throw on range, or treat a parse failure like a missing claim.

rules.statement: In production code, saturate rather than overflow when adding a margin to an instant near `DateTimeOffset.MaxValue`, or compare elapsed time instead (`now - instant - skew > limit`).
rules.why: Adding a margin to an attacker-supplied far-future instant can throw on overflow.
rules.check: `instant + margin` or `AddSeconds` on received instants without a saturation guard.

rules.statement: In production code, read a count of seconds a remote party sends (`expires_in`, `interval`) with a whole-number reader that accepts `60.0` or `6e1` but refuses fractions, strings and out-of-range values (or the matching JsonConverter), never `JsonElement.TryGetInt32` or the serializer's default int handling.
rules.why: JSON has one number type, so a peer may write a whole number in forms the BCL int readers reject.
rules.check: TryGetInt32/GetInt32 or plain `int` serialized members for remote-sent second counts.

rules.statement: In production code, stamp an instant that a JWT or stored grant carries with whole-second precision from `TimeProvider` (e.g. a GetUtcNowWithPrecisionInSeconds helper), not a raw `GetUtcNow()`.
rules.why: A stored time must equal the NumericDate it round-trips through.
rules.check: Raw TimeProvider.GetUtcNow()/DateTimeOffset.UtcNow used for token or grant timestamps.

rules.statement: In production code, never put a helper with a method body in an `*.Abstractions` package.
rules.why: Abstractions packages hold contracts only; implementations live in the implementation or foundation packages.
rules.check: Methods with bodies (extension methods, static helpers) added under *.Abstractions projects.

rules.statement: In production code, bound a received client-supplied JWT's lifetime through the validator's lifetime requirement (a max lifetime measured from the earliest asserted iat/nbf), never ad-hoc `exp` arithmetic, and keep its replay record until `exp` plus the effective clock skew rather than a fixed margin.
rules.why: Measuring from the earliest asserted start stops the client from gaming the cap, and a fixed replay margin can expire before the token does.
rules.check: Manual exp - now comparisons for client assertions or request objects, or replay caches with fixed TTLs.

rules.statement: In production code, validate a received JWT only through the central JWT validator, stating its whole policy: explicit allowed signature (and key-management, content-encryption, and empty compression) algorithms where an unset list permits nothing, and the recipient's decryption keys named explicitly.
rules.why: Unset-means-all would accept any algorithm, and the validator never infers keys; the policy must be stated by the caller.
rules.check: Hand-rolled JWT validation, algorithm lists read as 'unset means all', or missing decryption-key configuration.

rules.statement: In production code, never re-check a JWT's `alg` by hand after validation in place of the algorithm allow-list; an early check that only selects a precise error code is fine alongside it.
rules.why: A check after decoding runs after the cryptography it must precede.
rules.check: Post-validation comparisons of the alg header used as the security check.

rules.statement: In production code, fail token validation with a machine-readable failure code, and branch on why a token failed by reading the failure code, never the message text.
rules.why: Message text is for humans and can change; codes are set where the failure is detected.
rules.check: String comparisons or Contains on validation error messages, or Fail calls without a code.

rules.statement: In production code, protect a JWT addressed to a client with the algorithm the client registered and its published public key, within its effective supported ceilings, failing with `server_error` instead of substituting; never pick the first listed algorithm, encrypt to a tenant or shared key, or compress a server-produced JWT.
rules.why: Tokens must follow the client's registered metadata, and RFC 8725 §3.6 advises against compression.
rules.check: Algorithm selection via First(), encryption with server/tenant keys, or a zip header on produced JWTs.

rules.statement: In production code, write a key in a JOSE header (an `epk`, a DPoP `jwk`) with only its public members, and refuse a received header key that carries any private member.
rules.why: Anyone holding the token can read the header, so an ephemeral private key there discloses the content encryption key.
rules.check: Header key serialization that includes private parameters (d, p, q, k…), or received header keys accepted without a private-member check.

rules.statement: In production code, import a client's keys under one key policy through the central importer, and read a client's public keys from a single source (stored keys or jwks_uri, never both) through the central resolver; never use a JWK `kid` as a globally unique secret identifier, and match key types by `kty` through a catalog lookup, not a switch.
rules.why: Every entry point must apply the same policy (public only, consistent use/key_ops/alg, unique kid), and a kid is only the owner's name for a key.
rules.check: Direct secret-importer calls or stored-key reads for client keys, kid used as a secret id, switch statements over kty values.

rules.statement: In production code, read a client's TLS certificate only through the central certificate resolver, never `HttpContext.Connection.ClientCertificate` or a forwarded header directly, and treat a forwarded value that can't be decoded as `invalid_request`, not an absent certificate.
rules.why: Behind a proxy the connection's certificate is the proxy's, and a present-but-malformed credential must fail visibly.
rules.check: Direct uses of Connection.ClientCertificate or forwarded certificate headers; a decode failure mapped to null.

rules.statement: In production code, give a typed `Claim` its value in the declared type's XML Schema lexical form, formatting numbers with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, never culture-formatted.
rules.why: The claim-to-JSON mapping parses values strictly in their declared type; a culture-formatted value like "1,000" becomes a verbatim string.
rules.check: `new Claim(..., x.ToString(), ClaimValueTypes.Integer...)` without the invariant culture.

rules.statement: In production code, prefer an instance service behind an interface, registered as a singleton, to a static utility class, and minimize `static`.
rules.why: Production code must be unit-test-friendly, and static utilities can't be substituted.
rules.check: New static classes with behavior that collaborators depend on.

rules.statement: In production code, never capture request or ambient context in stored state; a type that reads ambient request data is a live view over `IHttpContextAccessor`.
rules.why: Captured context goes stale or leaks across requests and makes code hard to test.
rules.check: Fields storing HttpContext, the request or user values in singletons or long-lived objects.

rules.statement: In production code, constructor-inject every dependency; only a singleton needing a scoped or open-generic collaborator resolves it from `HttpContext.RequestServices` or `IServiceProvider` at the point of use.
rules.why: Constructor injection keeps code testable, and the point-of-use resolution remains testable through a real ServiceProvider.
rules.check: Service-locator calls outside that sanctioned case, or `new` of collaborators.

rules.statement: In production code, wrap an un-mockable dependency in a facade: an `internal interface` and an `internal sealed` forwarding implementation under a `Facades/` folder, with the passthrough implementation marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`.
rules.why: Facades make framework or static dependencies mockable without testing trivial passthroughs.
rules.check: Direct use of hard-to-mock APIs in logic, or facades misplaced, public, or missing the coverage exclusion.

rules.statement: In production code, use `internal virtual` as the local override seam for a helper or a factory method that allocates an object handed to a dependency, and extract an interface when the seam is reused or substantial.
rules.why: It is the sanctioned lightweight test seam.
rules.check: Ad-hoc seams such as public virtual methods or static hooks for testing.

rules.statement: In production code, leave internal implementation classes unsealed so tests can mock them, mock public types through their interfaces instead of adding `public virtual`, and don't ask to seal internal types for CA1852; `sealed` stays correct for data, options, event and facade-implementation types.
rules.why: CA1852 skips assemblies with InternalsVisibleTo, which every package grants its tests, and sealing internal services blocks mocking.
rules.check: Before suggesting `sealed` on an internal service, see whether the assembly grants InternalsVisibleTo; flag new public virtual members added only for mocking.

rules.statement: In production code, make sure every type or member that can carry `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` is either exercised by tests or annotated with it (with a one-line reason when non-obvious), excluding only thin passthroughs, DI registration wiring and framework-event adapters.
rules.why: Anything with behavior must be tested; only trivial infrastructure may be excluded.
rules.check: New behavioral code with no tests, or the exclusion attribute on code that has real logic.

rules.statement: In production code, keep the `## [Unreleased]` section of CHANGELOG.md matching the code in a change consumers can observe, and record such a change in an ADR before or with its pull request.
rules.why: A pre-release project describes the product as it is, and observable changes are decided before they are built.
rules.check: Pull requests that change observable behavior or public API without a CHANGELOG update or ADR.
